summaries.summary: Healthcare data and modern analytics offer opportunities to improve health services, personalised medicine, and NHS databases through advanced analytics.
The National Reporting and Learning System (NRLS), set up in 2003, contains more than 13 million patient safety incident reports with structured data and free text.
Structured NRLS data are routinely analysed, but free text is largely unused because manual reading is time-consuming and automatic categorisation methodologies are lacking.
The proposed unsupervised method combines deep neural-network text embeddings with multiscale Markov Stability (MS) community detection on a sparsified geometric similarity graph.
The methodology uses 13 million NRLS records for embedding and analyses 3229 records from St Mary's Hospital, London over three months in 2014.
The framework combines text-embedding, geometric graph construction and multi-resolution community detection to identify content-based clusters from free, unstructured text unsupervised.
The pipeline preprocesses text, trains Doc2Vec on 13 million records, infers vectors for 3229 documents, builds an MST-kNN graph, and applies Markov Stability.
The full dataset includes more than 13 million confidential NRLS reports from 2004 to 2016, with more than 170 features and 15 top-level categories.
Text preprocessing on all 13 million records uses NLTK tokenisation, punctuation and digit-only token removal, Porter or Snowball stemming, and stop-word removal.
The methodology avoids labelled data at the core of supervised or semi-supervised classification methods and uses vector representations of text documents.
Classical bag-of-words (Bow) methods use TF-iDF vectors but ignore word order, proximity, semantic and syntactic relationships, and are high-dimensional and sparse.
Distributed Bag of Words (DBOW), a Paragraph Vectors or Doc2Vec method, represents word sequences as d-dimensional vectors, typically d=500, and captures semantic and syntactic characterisations.
Gensim trained PV-DBOW models on 13 million, 1 million and 2 million NRLS records and 5 million Wikipedia articles to test corpus size and specificity.
Doc2Vec benchmarking used centroids for 15 hand-coded categories, 100 nearest reports per centroid, and counted incident reports out of 1500 correctly assigned.
The optimised Doc2Vec model uses 13+ million NRLS records, dbow, 300 dimensions, 10 epochs, window size 15, minimum count 5, 5 negative samples, and 0.001 down-sampling.
Doc2Vec infers vectors for N=3229 records, and a normalised cosine similarity matrix is constructed from pairwise cosine similarities and distances.
The fully connected weighted graph contains many weak, redundant edges that obscure graph structure in high-dimensional noisy datasets.
An MST-kNN graph sparsifies the normalised similarity matrix by combining a Kruskal minimum spanning tree with k nearest neighbours and weighting edges by similarity.
Figure 2 shows that the MST-kNN graph with k=13 balances local and global structure, while very small or large k values degrade robustness or coherence.
The analysis fixes k=13, after scanning k in [1,50] and finding robustness as long as k is not too small, i.e., k > 13.

MST-kNN is simple, robust and balances local and global structure, while alternative sparsification approaches include Graphical Lasso, Planar Maximally Filtered Graph, spectral sparsification and RMST.
Community detection finds partitions according to cost functions, and Markov Stability provides dynamics-based, multi-scale community detection using random walks of all lengths.
MS applies continuous-time diffusion to similarity graph A to find robust document clusters across Markov time t without a priori community numbers or organisation.
For adjacency matrix A, the random walk Laplacian L_RW=I_N-D^{-1}A defines P(t)=e^{-t L_RW}, and a membership matrix H maps N nodes into C clusters.
Equation 4 defines R(t,H)=H^T[Pi P(t)-pi pi^T]H as the clustered autocovariance matrix.
In R(t,H), pi is the steady-state distribution, Pi=diag(pi), and elements quantify random-walk community transition probabilities minus stationarity chance.
The cost function measuring partition goodness over time t is termed the Markov Stability of partition H.
Equation 5 defines r(t,H)=trace[R(t,H)] as the Markov Stability of partition H.
A partition H maximising r(t,H) has communities preserving flow within themselves over time t, with large diagonal and small off-diagonal elements of R(t,H).
MS uses Louvain 500 times per Markov time, selects the best 50 by r(t,H), and assesses robustness with VI(t) dips and VI(t,t') plateaus.

ForceAtlas2 BIBREF30 visualises the graph of 3229 NRLS Patient Incident reports, with colourings by hand-coded categories or multiscale MS communities indicating spatially consistent document clusters.

Sankey diagrams visualise node memberships across partitions and hand-coded categories, including two-layer diagrams for MS clusters and a multilayer diagram for multi-resolution MS community detection.

Heatmaps of normalised contingency (z-score) tables complement Sankey diagrams, comparing content clusters with external categories across resolution levels, quantified by the $NMI$ score in Eq. ( 8 ).
The method clusters text documents by intrinsic content as topic detection, and Word Clouds summarise clusters for evaluation, comparison with hand-coded categories, and practitioner monitoring.
For comprehensible word clouds, NLTK POS tagging retains adjectives, nouns, and verbs, removes common verbs, lemmatises residual words, and uses Python wordcloud with 2 or 3-gram frequency lists.
The hand-coded classification is not used as `ground truth'; cluster quality is quantified by intrinsic topic coherence and similarity to external hand-coded categories.
Pointwise mutual information ( $PMI$ ) BIBREF13 , BIBREF14 is an intrinsic information-theoretical score capturing the probability of words being used together in the same group of documents.
Eq. 6 defines $PMI(w_1,w_2)=\log {\frac{P(w_1 w_2)}{P(w_1)P(w_2)}}$.
Word probabilities and co-occurrence come from the corpus, and aggregate $\widehat{PMI}$ uses median $PMI$ between each cluster's 10 most common words and a weighted average.
Eq. 7 defines $\widehat{PMI} (C)$ as a size-weighted sum over clusters of median $PMI$ among word pairs in $S_i$.
In Eq. 7, $c_i$ denotes clusters in partition $C$ with size $n_i$, $N=\sum _{c_i \in C} n_i$ is total nodes, and $S_i$ is the top 10 words for cluster $c_i$.
The $\widehat{PMI}$ score evaluates partitions without labelled ground truth and has performed well against human interpretation of topics on different corpora.
Normalised mutual information ( $NMI$ ) compares external classification a posteriori by quantifying similarity between clusterings using correct and incorrect assignments.
Eq. 8 defines $NMI(C,D)$ as $I(C,D)$ divided by $\sqrt{H(C)H(D)}$, expanded using joint and marginal probabilities.
In Eq. 8, $I(C,D)$ is Mutual Information and $H(C)$ and $H(D)$ are the entropies of the two partitions.
$NMI$ is bounded $0 \le NMI \le 1$, with $NMI=1$ for perfect agreement, relates to V-measure, and compares MS and other partitions against hand-coded classification.
MS was applied over $t \in [0.01, 100]$ in steps of 0.01 to the MST-kNN graph of $N=3229$ records, with 500 Louvain optimisations and $VI(t)$ and $VI(t,t^{\prime })$ robustness assessments.

Figure 3 plots number of clusters and variation of information metrics, with long $VI(t,t^{\prime })$ plateaus and $VI(t)$ dips identifying robust partitions from 44 communities to 3 communities at five Markov times.

MS reveals rich multi-level partitions with strong quasi-hierarchical organisation, without imposing hierarchy a priori, enabling content-similar clusters at different granularity levels for practitioners.
The five resolution levels in Figure 3 were examined with lemmatised word clouds, Sankey diagrams, and contingency tables linking content clusters with hand-coded categories a posteriori.

The 44-community partition has well-defined clusters, finer than 15 hand-coded categories, with sub-themes, cross-category communities, and specific topics including blood transfusions, pressure ulcer, consent, mental health, and child protection.
The 12-community and 17-community levels near 15 hand-coded categories show aggregation from the 44-way partition, including Accidents, Nursing, Medication, and Homecare medication.

Communities 10 and 11 span `Documentation' and `Clinical Assessment', community 9 spans `Admission/Transfer' and `Infrastructure', and other communities separate `Treatment/Procedure' records into medically coherent groups.
The 7-way partition preserves Radiotherapy, Pressure ulcer and Labour ward, while the 3-way partition contains accidents, procedural matters, and labour ward.
Figure 8 shows word clouds explicitly illustrating agglomeration of content from sub-themes into larger themes for the 17, 12 and 7-way partitions.
Robustness was examined for Doc2Vec embeddings instead of BoW vectors, Doc2Vec training corpus size, MST-kNN sparsity, and comparisons with LDA-BoW and other community detection methods.
Doc2Vec is integral to the pipeline, producing lower dimensional vectors than BoW with higher semantic and syntactic content and reported advantages in semantic similarity benchmarks.
A TF-iDF MST-kNN graph analysed with MS showed in Figure 7 that Doc2Vec outperforms BoW across all resolutions in $NMI$ and $\widehat{PMI}$ scores.
Table 1 tests Doc2Vec training sets of 1 million and 2 million records from $\sim $ 13 million records, with Figure S3 showing performance only mildly affected by training set size.
Figure S4 shows $NMI$ and $\widehat{PMI}$ scores reach similar quality for $k$ above 13-16, with minor improvement afterward, favouring a relatively small but not too small $k$.
Table 2 shows MS and five LDA models give comparably similar partitions to hand-coded categories by $NMI$, while MS has higher $\widehat{PMI}$ topic coherence across all scales.
The method takes approximately 13 hours total, including Doc2Vec on 13 million records (11 hours) and 400 partitions (2 hours), while 5 LDA models require 30 hours.
LDA computes topics at a pre-determined resolution, whereas MS obtains partitions at all resolutions in one Markov time sweep and selects relevant partitions by robustness.

Figure S5 compares MS with Modularity Optimisation BIBREF44 , InfoMap BIBREF4 , Walktrap BIBREF45 , Label Propagation BIBREF46 , and Multi-resolution Louvain BIBREF35 , showing improved or equal $NMI$ and $\widehat{PMI}$ across all scales except Infomap above 50 clusters.
Markov Stability with paragraph vectors and a similarity graph extracts unsupervised content-based clusters from healthcare safety incident reports at multiple resolutions.
A posteriori analysis against hand-coded categories and intrinsic topic coherence showed meaningful clusters, including Labour ward, Pressure ulcer, Chemotherapy, and Radiotherapy.
Level 1 categories vary in size, while multi-scale partitioning finds corresponding content groups and medical subcategories, with future work on Level 2, around 100 categories, and WHO ICPS.
Free text analysis provides timely intelligible incident report categories from reporters' words, adding rich information and a complementary axis to pre-defined classes.
Free text analytical approaches could free risk managers' time from classification and correction, and discover emerging topics using projection, anomaly detection, and innovation detection.

Ongoing work examines comparisons across healthcare organisations, change over time, in-class text similarities, dynamic embedding updates, robust graph construction, anomaly detection, and online classification suggestions.
The NRLS incident report dataset is managed by BDAU, Imperial College London, analysed in its Secure Environment, and cannot be publicised beyond the manuscript.
The authors declare that they have no competing interests.
Abbreviations include NHS, NRLS, BoW, LDA, Doc2Vec, MST, kNN, MS, NLTK, TF-iDF, PV, DBOW, VI, NMI, and PMI.
MTA conducted computational research; MTA and MB analysed data and designed the framework; MB, EM and SNY conceived the study; all authors wrote the manuscript.
